notes: Employment tribunal amendment appeal; Selkent and Quarcoopome analysis is detailed though largely procedural.

enrichment.short_title: Ali v ONS: employment tribunal amendment and indirect race discrimination
key_facts: Mr Ali, a black candidate of African origin, complained to the Employment Tribunal that the Office for National Statistics discriminated against him in recruitment.
After a remitted hearing he sought to amend his originating application to add an indirect discrimination claim based on an internal-candidate preference policy disclosed during proceedings.
The tribunal held no amendment was needed because paragraphs 3 and 7 already pleaded indirect discrimination; the EAT disagreed and remitted the amendment application.

On appeal the Court of Appeal held the proposed paragraph 25A pleaded a new claim and section 68(6) applied, but the just-and-equitable and Selkent hardship tests would reach the same result on these facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on whether an employment tribunal should allow a late amendment to add indirect racial discrimination after remittal from the EAT.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; amendment application remitted with direction that section 68(6) applies and no direction that the amendment does not raise a new cause of action.
enrichment.ratio: A general claim of race discrimination in an originating application does not necessarily include indirect discrimination under section 1(1)(b); where a new claim is added out of time section 68(6) applies, but on facts such as these the Selkent balance-of-hardship test and the just-and-equitable test should produce the same outcome.
legal_issues: Whether paragraphs 3 and 7 of the originating application already pleaded indirect discrimination
Whether Quarcoopome remains good law after Smith v Zeneca and Housing Corporation v Bryant
Whether section 68(6) or the Selkent injustice-and-hardship test governs the amendment application
Whether the court should direct that the amendment does not raise a new cause of action
linked_authorities: Selkent Bus Co Ltd v Moore [1996] IRLR 661
Quarcoopome v Sockshop Holdings Ltd [1995] IRLR 353
Smith v Zeneca (Agrochemicals) Ltd [2000] ICR 800
Housing Corporation v Bryant [1999] ICR 123

confidence.notes: Procedural ratio and remittal directions are clearly stated; amendment outcome on remittal remains for the tribunal.

notes: Landmark Iraqi Kurd asylum policy case; Davis J quashed refusal and granted declaratory relief with permission to appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Rashid v SSHD: failure to apply KAZ relocation policy and refugee status
key_facts: Bakhtear Rashid, an Iraqi Kurd from government-controlled Iraq, claimed asylum in December 2001 and was refused partly on internal relocation to the Kurdish Autonomous Zone.
Unknown to him and his advisers, a Home Office policy from October 2000 generally disavowed reliance on KAZ relocation for applicants from Ba'athist-controlled areas.

Comparable claimants Maghdeed and Anwar were granted refugee status in March 2003 when the policy surfaced, but Rashid's case was delayed through the Iraq war and then refused on post-war country conditions.
The Secretary of State conceded that had the policy been applied when Rashid applied he would have been granted refugee status and indefinite leave to remain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of post-war refusal letters after an earlier stacked challenge was withdrawn; permission to appeal granted at the hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Decision letters of 16 January and 5 August 2004 quashed; declaratory relief that Rashid should be accorded refugee status and indefinite leave to remain; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where the Secretary of State wrongly failed to apply an established asylum policy that would have granted refugee status, he cannot later rely on changed country conditions caused by intervening delay to deny the claimant the benefit of equal treatment; such unfairness may require departure from the Ravichandran contemporaneity principle.
legal_issues: Whether failure to apply the KAZ non-relocation policy amounted to abuse of power or breach of legitimate expectation
Whether post-2003 changed conditions in Iraq justified refusing refugee status
Whether detrimental reliance on the policy was required
Whether Ravichandran permits the Secretary of State to profit from his own failure to apply policy
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Ravichandran [1996] Imm AR 97
R v North and East Devon Health Authority, ex parte Coughlan [2001] QB 213
R v Newham London Borough Council, ex parte Bibi [2003] 1 WLR 237

confidence.notes: Concessions, facts and final declaratory relief are comprehensively reasoned on the particular facts.

notes: Personal injury mitigation appeal; Gage LJ's cumulative evaluation analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Edmonds v Lloyds TSB: refusal of back injections and mitigation of loss
key_facts: Mrs Edmonds tripped at work and suffered a persistent sacro-coccygeal soft tissue injury that prevented her return to employment.
Consultant Mr Osborne recommended three hydrocortisone injections under general anaesthetic with about a 50% chance of significant improvement, but she declined after GP advice and anxiety.
The county court judge found she failed to mitigate and reduced damages on that basis.
The Court of Appeal held the judge failed to evaluate cumulatively her credible reasons for refusing treatment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court personal injury trial where liability was apportioned 75/25 and mitigation was the central issue.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on mitigation; damages remitted to a district judge for reassessment of general and special damages including loss of congenial employment.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a claimant acted reasonably in refusing recommended medical treatment is fact-specific; a trial judge must give proper cumulative weight to unchallenged patient reasons including GP advice, fear of spinal injection, absence of guaranteed success and the treating surgeon's acceptance that refusal was reasonable.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant unreasonably failed to mitigate by refusing epidural-style injections
Whether the judge properly weighed GP advice and patient anxiety
Whether Mr Osborne's 50% improvement estimate was overstated as a prospect of recovery
Assessment of loss of earnings and care after successful mitigation appeal

confidence.notes: Mitigation finding reversed clearly; quantum remains for remittal.

notes: Handling stolen goods case stated; ownership averment and recent possession doctrine clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Iqbal v DPP: handling conviction quashed for ownership and recent possession flaws

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Police stopped Mohammed Iqbal's car and found a laptop; he and his passenger gave conflicting accounts of ownership before any caution.
The prosecution case at trial depended on proving the laptop was stolen from Daimler Chrysler where Iqbal worked as a security guard.
The magistrates convicted of handling stolen goods and drew an adverse inference from his failure to give evidence.
On case stated the Crown conceded there was insufficient evidence the laptop belonged to Daimler Chrysler.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' conviction for handling stolen goods.
enrichment.outcome: Pre-caution roadside conversation rightly admitted; appeal allowed on questions (b) and (c); conviction quashed with no remittal.
enrichment.ratio: Where ownership of stolen goods is an integral part of the prosecution case and the defendant does not give evidence because no-case was rejected on that basis, the conviction cannot be upheld on the basis of theft from persons unknown; recent possession doctrine also requires proof of a recent theft from the alleged source.
legal_issues: Admissibility of pre-caution roadside answers under PACE section 78 and Code C
Whether ownership in Daimler Chrysler was a material averment
Whether conviction could stand without proof of ownership
Whether section 35 adverse inference was available on an insufficiently strong case
linked_authorities: R v Deakin [1972] 3 All ER 803

confidence.notes: Three case-stated questions answered explicitly with Crown concession on ownership.

notes: Local plan section 287 challenge; Sullivan J's housing-reasons adequacy analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Secondsite v Poole: adequacy of reasons for rejecting inspector's housing allocation

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Secondsite owned a former British Gas site allocated for employment in Poole's local plan first alteration.
An inspector recommended reallocating the site to housing because of concerns about housing yield and surplus employment land, but the council refused.
The claimant challenged under section 287, arguing the council failed to grapple with the inspector's housing-flexibility reasoning.
The council maintained its housing allocations would meet the structure plan requirement and that employment land should be retained for choice and range.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 287 application to quash adopted housing and employment chapters of the Poole Local Plan First Alteration.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; council's statement and responses adequately addressed the inspector's underlying concern about Phase 1 housing yield.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 27/28 reasons must grapple with an inspector's recommendation; where the inspector expresses only a general tentative concern that Phase 1 housing yield could be optimistic, a council may adequately respond by explaining why experience of sites coming forward gives confidence without detailed site-by-site analysis.
legal_issues: Whether the council adequately reasoned against reallocating the Bourne Valley site from employment to housing
Whether employment-side reasons were sufficient at both regulation 27 and 28 stages
Whether reference to sites where implementation was commencing was a fatal inaccuracy
Application of Stirk and Bainbridge on adequacy of local plan reasons
linked_authorities: Westminster City Council v Great Portland Estates plc [1985] 1 AC 661
Bainbridge v Hambleton District Council [2000] 80 P&CR 61
Stirk v Bridgnorth District Council [1997] 73 P&CR 479

confidence.notes: Housing-reasons conclusion is clear though employment reasoning was conceded adequate only at the responses stage.

notes: Section 18 appeal; plea-offer cross-examination and fresh witness leave issues clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: R v Hayes: admissibility of solicitor's section 47 plea offer at wounding trial
key_facts: Hayes was convicted by a 10-2 majority of section 18 wounding with intent after allegedly kicking or stamping on David Barry's head in Amesbury.
His solicitors had offered before trial to plead guilty to section 47 ABH excluding head injuries, consistent with his police interview.
The judge allowed cross-examination on the offer under section 78; the jury asked about the letter after retiring.
Hayes also sought leave to add fresh evidence from Stephanie McPhie, whom he had chosen not to call at trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by certificate against conviction for wounding with intent; application for leave to add fresh evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-examination on the plea offer was admissible and not unfair; leave to add McPhie's evidence refused.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor's written offer to plead guilty to section 47 may be put in cross-examination as a previous inconsistent statement where it is relevant to credibility and section 78 fairness is not engaged; under section 23(2) fresh evidence will not be admitted where the defendant deliberately chose not to call an available witness at trial.
legal_issues: Whether cross-examination on a rejected section 47 plea offer was admissible and fair
Effect of jury questions about the solicitor's letter
Whether Stephanie McPhie's evidence was capable of belief and could afford grounds to allow the appeal
Whether there was a reasonable explanation for not calling McPhie at trial
index_terms: deliberate decision not to call witness
linked_authorities: R v Hampton and Brown [2004] EWCA Crim 2139

confidence.notes: Both appeal grounds analysed in detail with clear dismissal.

notes: Gypsy green-belt injunction timing appeal; 2-1 Court of Appeal on proportionality of short compliance period.

enrichment.short_title: Coates v South Bucks: gypsy caravan injunction compliance period and Article 8
key_facts: Gypsies and Irish Travellers occupied a sensitive green belt site at Bellswood Lane in breach of planning controls and court orders.
The council obtained a mandatory injunction; the dispute was whether compliance should be suspended for one month or until planning permission was determined.
The site had a long history of failed planning applications, deliberate breaches of interim orders and no valid planning application at trial.
Penry-Davey J granted one month's suspension (two months for one appellant); Sedley LJ granted permission to appeal on timing only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on the proportionality under Article 8 of the short period allowed before an agreed mandatory planning injunction took effect.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority; one-month (and two-month) compliance periods upheld, extended to November/December 2004 in the order.
enrichment.ratio: Where travellers unlawfully occupy a highly sensitive green belt site with a history of enforcement defeats and contumacious breach of court orders, and planning permission is unlikely, a short suspension before a mandatory injunction operates is a proportionate interference with Article 8 rights even though hardship will result.
legal_issues: Whether immediate eviction pending a called-in planning decision was proportionate under Article 8
How a judge should structure reasons where proportionality is in issue
Relevance of flagrant breach of court orders and poor planning prospects
Whether delay in lodging a planning application weakened the stay argument
linked_authorities: South Bucks District Council v Porter [2003] 2 WLR 1547
First Secretary of State v Chichester DC [2004] EWCA Civ 1248

confidence.notes: Majority outcome and Article 8 balancing are clear; Sedley LJ dissent on deferral until planning inquiry.

notes: Confiscation transitional jurisdiction appeal; Simpson interpretation applied to abandoned pre-1995 count.

enrichment.short_title: R v Aslam: Proceeds of Crime Act 1995 jurisdiction after abandoning pre-commencement count
key_facts: Aslam pleaded guilty to numerous dishonesty offences including fraud with stolen credit cards and false benefit claims.
Confiscation proceedings under the 1995 Act included one pre-1 November 1995 count and one similar offence taken into consideration.
The Crown abandoned reliance on the pre-commencement count at the hearing after the defence raised section 16(5).
Judge Birtles made a £25,000 confiscation order including course-of-conduct amounts under the post-1995 regime.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave against a confiscation order on transitional jurisdiction under section 16(5) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; court had jurisdiction under the 1995 Act once the Crown abandoned the pre-commencement count at the confiscation hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Section 16(5) prevents use of the 1995 confiscation regime only where a pre-commencement offence in the same proceedings remains one in respect of which a confiscation order is sought; abandonment of such a count at the hearing is analogous to offering no evidence and does not destroy jurisdiction over post-commencement counts.
legal_issues: Construction of section 16(5) after R v Simpson
Whether abandoning a pre-1995 count at the confiscation hearing was an abuse of process
Whether an offence taken into consideration triggers section 16(5)
Whether course-of-conduct confiscation under section 72AA was available
linked_authorities: R v Simpson [2004] QB 118
R v Sekhon [2003] 1 WLR 1655

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional point and dismissal clearly reasoned on transitional construction.

notes: SENDIST disability threshold appeal; substantial means more than trivial is central.

enrichment.short_title: M v SW School: SENDIST disability finding quashed for pupil A
key_facts: Mr and Mrs M appealed for their daughter A after the SENDIST dismissed a disability discrimination claim against SW School.
The claim concerned refusal to allow automatic transfer into Year 3 and alleged discrimination related to vision, mobility and speech difficulties.
Expert reports from optometrists and educational psychologists were before the tribunal.
The tribunal found A was not disabled because difficulties were not substantial and long-term, including because glasses corrected vision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 11 appeal to the High Court on points of law from a SENDIST disability discrimination decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision quashed and remitted to a differently constituted SENDIST; anonymity order made.
enrichment.ratio: Substantial adverse effect for DDA purposes means more than minor or trivial; a SENDIST must apply that test separately to each relevant capacity, explain rejection of expert evidence and not treat school functioning as displacing the statutory focus on inability to carry out day-to-day activities.
legal_issues: Correct meaning of substantial adverse effect under section 1 DDA 1995
Whether corrected vision by glasses excludes impairment
Whether tribunal reasons adequately dealt with expert evidence on vision, mobility and speech
Appropriate reasons and procedural fairness on specialist tribunal appeals
linked_authorities: Goodwin v Patent Office [1999] ICR 302
McNicol v Balfour Beatty [2002] ICR 1498
H v R School and the SENDIST [2004] EWHC 981 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Legal errors identified without rehearing merits; remittal for fresh disability and merits findings.

notes: Share purchase warranty notice appeal; clause 3(o) construction and service on company analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Bottin v Venson: share purchase warranty notice and misrepresentation bar
key_facts: Bottin invested £10 million in Venson Group plc preference shares under a December 1999 share purchase agreement with extensive warranties.
Venson had forecast strong 1999-2000 profits but suffered large losses; Bottin served a December 2002 clause 3(o) breach-of-warranty notice.
Peter Smith J struck out the warranty claim for inadequate notice and limited any misrepresentation claim to negligent statements in the October and December forecasts.
The Court of Appeal held personal service on Venson was effective via the receptionist and most of the notice was sufficient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from summary judgment/striking out and permission to amend in a warranty and misrepresentation dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: December notice valid except forecast-related paragraphs; warranty misrepresentation route barred; clause 16(d) issue deferred to trial; cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A clause 3(o) warranty notice need only specify details of the event or circumstances giving rise to the claim available at the time, not full pleading-level particulars of knowledge; treating warranties as representations for a damages claim does not avoid notice and limitation conditions in the agreement.
legal_issues: Whether the December 2002 notice was personally served on Venson under clause 19
Whether the notice satisfied clause 3(o) detail and estimate requirements
Whether Bottin could sue for misrepresentation based on warranted documents
Whether clause 16(d) contractually excluded non-agreement representations
linked_authorities: Senate Electrical Wholesalers Ltd v STC Submarine Systems Ltd [1999] 2 Lloyd's Rep 423
Watford Electronics Ltd v Sanderson CFL Ltd [2001] 1 All ER (Comm) 696

confidence.notes: Notice validity and misrepresentation bar clearly decided; clause 16(d) left for trial.
